q: Which situation most clearly calls for a co-founder rather than a freelancer or an adviser?
options: You'd like company while you work, and a friend has offered to help out on weekends.
The core of the business is work you can't do yourself, and it needs a long-term owner.
You need a logo and a landing page designed before your launch next month.
You'd like someone to share the cost of the tools and subscriptions you pay for.
why: A co-founder shares responsibility for the whole company over years. One-off tasks and occasional help can usually come from a freelancer, an adviser or a later hire.

q: You're a developer building a tool for restaurant owners. Which potential co-founder probably adds the most?
options: Another strong developer you enjoyed working with at your last job.
A well-known investor who has offered to make introductions for you.
A friend who loves the idea but can't give it any time for a year.
A former restaurant manager who has sold to restaurants and wants the same pace as you.
why: Look for skills that complement yours and values that match. A second developer duplicates what you already do, and enthusiasm without time doesn't move the company forward.

q: You've met someone promising and you get along well. What's the most useful next step before either of you commits?
options: Do a small project together with a clear finish, such as ten customer interviews in three weeks.
Agree on an equity split now, while you're both still excited about the idea.
Register the company together so that you both feel properly committed.
Meet for coffee every week for a few months to get to know each other better.
why: Real work shows how someone follows through, communicates and handles disagreement. Equity and incorporation should wait until you know you can work well together.

q: When you pitch the idea to a potential co-founder, how should you handle what's still uncertain?
options: Leave it out for now and share the risks once they've committed.
Mention the risks only if they ask you about them directly.
Say plainly what's unproven, what joining will cost them, and that it may fail.
Replace it with a forecast showing how large the market could become.
why: Someone deciding whether to give up time and income deserves the full picture. People who join because of hype are more likely to leave when reality arrives.

q: A team uses a common vesting schedule: four years with a one-year cliff. A founder holding 30% of the shares leaves after six months. What typically happens to those shares?
options: They keep all 30%, because the shares were issued to them on day one.
They usually keep none, because nothing vests until the one-year cliff.
They keep 3.75%, because 6 of the 48 months have passed.
They keep 15%, because they finished half of the first year.
why: Under this common structure nothing vests before the cliff, so the company can usually buy back all of those shares. Real terms vary by agreement and country, which is why a lawyer should review yours.
